title: Single-character multilingual tokens vs English function tokens
explanation_markdown: The Group feature fires on isolated single-character tokens and punctuation across scripts (e.g., Vietnamese 'ế', Greek letters ν/ι, single-letter initials and dots), reflecting tokenization boundaries that isolate non‑ASCII or single-letter characters. The Baseline feature instead captures common English function tokens and orthographic separators (e.g., 'of', '-' and capital initials like 'W' or 'U'), so the two features cover different token types with low overlap.

title: Group-SAE: structural/section tokens vs Baseline-SAE: legal named entities
explanation_markdown: The Group-SAE feature (layer 13) activates on structural and formatting tokens — punctuation and symbols (')', '$') and document-section words like “equation”, “code”, “provision”, “declaration”, “opinion” — i.e., tokens that mark formal structure across domains (math, code, legal). The Baseline-SAE feature (also layer 13) instead focuses on named actors and organizations common in legal text ("Defender", "attorney", judge/party names like "Friedman", "Jackson", "distributor"). The moderate Jaccard (0.356) reflects some overlap in legal/formal contexts but a clear split between structural markers versus entity/actor recognition.

title: Numeric/token detector: coordinates and tabular numbers
explanation_markdown: High Jaccard (0.782) indicates these two features largely overlap: both respond to numeric tokens occurring in coordinates, measurement tables, and short numeric fields (e.g., x/y coordinates, accuracy/acc columns, and numeric lists). The Group-SAE feature is slightly broader — it activates on a wider set of numeric tokens (40, 80, 990 in addition to 20/30/70), suggesting sensitivity to a wider numeric range or multi-digit tokens — whereas the Baseline-SAE concentrates more on a smaller set (notably 70, 30, 20) and appears in contexts like hex/ascii byte sequences and repeated measurement columns.

title: Pronoun-focused feature capturing 'he' variants and tokenization artifacts
explanation_markdown: Both features strongly overlap (Jaccard 0.752) and appear to detect the third-person masculine pronoun in its surface forms ("he", "He", "him") as well as punctuation- or tokenizer-attached variants (">He", repeated "he he", and broken forms like "he ms"). Contexts show sentence-initial uses, embedded mentions, and informal/repeated tokens, so the features primarily encode pronoun identity plus sensitivity to capitalization and token-boundary artifacts; differences between Group-SAE and Baseline-SAE are minimal and mostly reflect minor ordering or boundary sensitivity.

title: Single-letter token detector: Group is sharper, Baseline is broader
explanation_markdown: Both features respond to the letter tokens 'S' and 's' (high Jaccard 0.848), indicating sensitivity to single-letter tokens appearing as sentence initials, headings, code variables, or standalone symbols. The Group-SAE (feature 5205, layer 14) is more specific to standalone single-letter occurrences and preserves case distinction. The Baseline-SAE (feature 310, layer 13) overlaps with that behavior but is noisier/broader — it also activates on short subword fragments like 'sc' and 'e' and on punctuation-adjacent pieces, suggesting a less focused, more surface-fragment representation.

title: Single-letter math-token detector — group picks structural symbols, baseline picks generic variables
explanation_markdown: Both features strongly overlap and detect single-character math tokens in LaTeX/math contexts (high Jaccard). The Group-SAE (layer 14) is biased toward uppercase/structural symbols and labeled objects (R, B, H, L, p, g) that name sets, matrices, operators or constants, suggesting a focus on semantic/math-structure tokens. The Baseline-SAE (layer 13) covers many of the same tokens but leans more toward lowercase variable/index names (s, x, a, i) and general-purpose math variables, indicating a more surface-level variable detector at a neighboring layer.

The Baseline feature instead activates on short, cross-linguistic surface tokens and orthographic pieces (single letters, diacritics, and short function words like i, ā, o, kad, Ak), showing a multilingual/orthography-oriented pattern rather than a coherent syntactic class. The low Jaccard (0.316) matches this shift from a language-specific syntactic signal to a heterogeneous orthographic signal.

title: Both/both — coordinating determiner

explanation_markdown: The Group-SAE (layer 15) activates on a variety of short subword fragments and affix-like sequences (e.g., as, aj, ids, ji, el and single-letter ī/ē), suggesting it represents morphological or lexical pieces. The Baseline-SAE (layer 13) mainly responds to isolated Latvian diacritic vowels (ā, ē, ī), indicating a more character-level/orthographic signal. The higher-layer group feature is therefore more specialized toward meaningful subword units, while the baseline is a more generic character detector.

title: Shared subword n-grams: clean suffix/morpheme detector (Group) vs. noisier mixed-token detector (Baseline)

The Baseline-SAE (layer 14) also captures those short n-grams but includes longer, more idiosyncratic substrings and code/token fragments ("inche", "ke", "ande"), making it a noisier, mixed-purpose detector.
